title: No agreement on buying 100% US agriculture, energy – Palace
summary: The Philippines has not reached a deal with the United States on sourcing its agriculture and energy supplies, Malacañang clarified yesterday, following business groups’ concerns over…

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 12:00am
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and US President Donald Trump troop the line during the arrival honors ceremony for Trump’s state visit at the Malacañang Palace on November 18, 2026
The STAR / Noel Pabalate

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has not reached a deal with the United States on sourcing its agriculture and energy supplies, Malacañang clarified yesterday, following business groups’ concerns over the announcement that Manila has agreed to buy all its requirements from Washington.

American President Donald Trump claimed last Saturday that President Marcos had agreed to buy 100 percent of the Philippines’ agricultural and energy supplies from the US during their bilateral meeting in Manila.
However, Marcos did not mention an arrangement to source all the Philippines’ agriculture and energy supplies from the US in a media interview in China a day earlier.
The President even highlighted the need to diversify supply sources to minimize risks arising from geopolitical tensions.

Business chambers in the Philippines have urged the Marcos administration to clarify its trade deal with the US, saying the Philippines should not be reliant on a single supplier and should not be compelled to purchase costlier goods.
“There are no terms yet,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said at a media briefing yesterday.

“No details and transactions have been discussed. What was discussed was fast-tracking the possible transactions, speeding up the work from the representative of the Philippines and the representative of the US,” Castro added.
She gave assurance that Marcos would not enter into a deal that would be disadvantageous to the Philippines and its citizens.
Meanwhile, the Department of Foreign Affairs was caught off guard by Trump’s claim, a senator admitted yesterday during plenary debates on the DFA’s proposed P35.2-billion budget for 2027.

Responding to interpellations by Sen. Imee Marcos, DFA budget sponsor Sen. Erwin Tulfo said while DFA officials attended the bilateral meeting between Trump and Marcos during the ASEAN summit, earlier discussions had focused strictly on tariffs.
“Actually, Sen. Imee, everybody was taken aback because this issue was only brought up during the bilateral meeting between the two presidents during the ASEAN,” Tulfo said.
“Prior to this, their discussions were all about tariffs, and there were no issues about importation of agricultural products and any other items,” he added.

Senator Marcos called the lack of prior consultation with foreign policy experts “alarming,” saying Tulfo’s remarks amounted to an admission that the DFA was sidelined despite the geopolitical implications of Trump’s statement.

“I think there’s an admission on the part of the DFA that they were kept in the dark regarding this announcement and that here on after, the matters have been assigned to others. The question that arises of course is who is formulating foreign policy if not the DFA,” Senator Marcos said.
She also flagged what she described as a warning attached to Trump’s remarks.

Tulfo clarified that Malacañang has assigned the trade and agricultural aspects of the matter to the Department of Trade and Industry and the Department of Agriculture, though the DFA continues to monitor developments and awaits further answers from its US counterparts.
The Senate subsequently approved the proposed 2027 budget of the DFA and its attached agencies in plenary. — Neil Jayson Servallos, EJ Macababbad
